# What open DAS tools exist?

## The tools

![](../figures/v030_funnel.png){fig-align="center" width=59%}

::: {.notes}
{{< meta n.funnel.candidates >}} candidates from forge search, registries and the
literature. Every one leaves by exactly one route. What survives is
{{< meta n.funnel.in_scope >}} DAS projects, plus
{{< meta n.funnel.supporting >}} seismology tools that also support DAS and
{{< meta n.funnel.other_fiber >}} for temperature or strain.
:::

## The tools

![](../figures/v020_totals.png){fig-align="center" width=98%}

::: {.notes}
{{< meta n.ecosystem_totals.projects >}} projects,
{{< meta n.ecosystem_totals.contributors >}} contributors,
{{< meta n.ecosystem_totals.commits >}} commits,
{{< meta n.ecosystem_totals.lines >}} lines,
{{< meta n.ecosystem_totals.citations >}} citations.

Citations cover only {{< meta n.ecosystem_totals.cited_projects >}} of the
projects, so that one is a floor. Lines of code is the softest number — a few
repositories carry vendored content — so lead with projects and commits if
pushed.
:::

## DAS4Whales

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
- Matched-filter and spectrogram whale-call detection
- Call association, localisation and track building
- Bathymetry and cable-geometry mapping
- The deepest end-to-end marine workflow of the five
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
![](assets/logo_das4whales.png){fig-align="center" width=88%}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Strengths first, then the logo. Say what it is for, not what it lacks.
:::

## DASCore

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
- Immutable patches with named coordinates and Pint units
- Spools index a directory, so you read only what you select
- Over 20 format families, with versioned handlers
- Entry-point plugins for readers and namespaces
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
![](assets/logo_dascore.png){fig-align="center" width=88%}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Strengths first, then the logo. Say what it is for, not what it lacks.
:::

## DASPy

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
- The richest seismology algorithm set of the five
- Curvelet denoising, decomposition, strain-to-velocity
- A simple Section and Collection workflow
- MIT — the lowest licensing friction
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
![](assets/logo_daspy.png){fig-align="center" width=88%}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Strengths first, then the logo. Say what it is for, not what it lacks.
:::

## Lightguide

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
- The published adaptive frequency–wavenumber denoiser
- Rust-backed, parallel, and fast
- Phase following along the fibre
- Green's-function forward modelling through Pyrocko
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
![](assets/logo_lightguide.png){fig-align="center" width=88%}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Strengths first, then the logo. Say what it is for, not what it lacks.
:::

## xdas

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
- Virtual arrays across thousands of files
- Compact coordinates instead of dense index arrays
- Stateful pipelines that survive chunk boundaries
- Live acquisition over ZeroMQ
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
![](assets/logo_xdas.png){fig-align="center" width=88%}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Strengths first, then the logo. Say what it is for, not what it lacks.
:::

# What are the gaps and opportunities?

## Interoperability

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
Five data models, five I/O layers, five ways to say the same thing.

- Overlap is how a field finds out what works
- The cost lands on the user, not the author
- Only paid when the tools cannot talk to each other
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
![](assets/interoperability.png){.fragment fig-align="center" width="94%"}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Say the concession first and mean it: five independent designs is how a field
finds out what works. Unidas is the existence proof that the conversion can be
written once instead of five times.
:::

## GPU and beyond NumPy

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
The shared layer is NumPy. Acceleration is bolted on one project at a time.

- Sixteen reach for PyTorch, eight for Dask, three for CuPy
- None of it is portable — the Array API is the target
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
![](assets/gpu.png){.fragment fig-align="center" width="88%"}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
65 of the 66 Python projects declare NumPy, and none of the five infrastructure
packages depends on an accelerator library beyond Numba and Dask. Plenty of
individual projects reach for PyTorch or CuPy -- the PyTorch bar is on the
dependency slide -- but each does it its own way, so nothing moves between them.
:::

## Metadata

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="46%"}
Every project invents its own station, channel and geometry fields.

- Seismology solved this once, with an inventory
- Fiber needs the same thing, not a sixth dialect
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
![](assets/metadata.png){.fragment fig-align="center" width="98%"}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
One integrated, reusable inventory. The right-hand sketch is what that could
look like: the point-sensor hierarchy on the left, the fiber one beside it.
:::

## Large-scale visualisation

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
Seven viewers in the census. Nothing in it depends on any of them.

- Multi-resolution, streaming, annotation — each solved separately
- The one gap where more tools has not meant more capability
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
[?]{.question-mark}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="beamer"}
```{=latex}
\vfill\begin{center}{\fontsize{100}{120}\selectfont\color{inerisblue}?}\end{center}\vfill
```
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Not for want of effort: MultiResViewer, FiLark, DAS_NIDF, DASexplorer, Xpick,
DASSourceLocator and DerZug are all in the census, and several are named on the
network slide. Not one of them is a dependency of anything else. The question
mark is which the field converges on, not whether anyone is trying.
:::

## Agents using what we have

![](../figures/p1_scientist_agent.png){fig-align="center" width=70%}

- Readable interfaces, stable contracts, honest errors

::: {.notes}
The tools we write now are the tools agents will use. This slide is about the
code that already exists: make it legible and predictable and an agent can
drive it. Nothing here is agent-ready yet.
:::

## Software we have not written yet

::: {.nonincremental}
Not porting a library for an agent to call — asking what software looks like
when an agent is the one writing and running it.
:::

![](../figures/p1_scientist_agent_oss.png){.fragment fig-align="center" width=58%}

::: {.notes}
The second half of the argument, and the speculative one. Say plainly that this
is where I think the field goes, not where it is.
:::

## Conclusions

- A young field: 76 of {{< meta n.ecosystem_totals.projects >}} projects began in 2020 or later
- Most build on NumPy, not on each other
- Five tools already cover five different jobs
- Interoperate rather than re-implement

::: {.notes}
Close on the call to action: publish it, declare your dependencies, and reuse a
data model rather than inventing a sixth.
:::

- Declare your dependencies; reuse a data model rather than inventing a sixth

is the cheapest thing in this talk to fix.
